33-024.r: Antibiotics → mostly obtained from bacteria: Streptomyces and other actinomycetes (soil bacteria) and Bacillus species; they kill bacteria or stop their growth.

33-025.r: Antibiotics among options → penicillin and sulfadiazine, so 'more than one'; aspirin and paracetamol are analgesic and antipyretic.

33-026.r: Antibiotic → penicillin. Aspirin, paracetamol → analgesic and antipyretic; chloroquine → antimalarial.

33-027.r: Wrong pair: antiseptic – aspirin → aspirin (acetylsalicylic acid) is analgesic, antipyretic, anti-inflammatory. Correct: antipyretic – paracetamol; antirachitic – calciferol (vitamin D).

33-028.r: Wrong pair: aspirin – anaesthetic → aspirin is analgesic and antipyretic. Correct: chloromycetin – antityphoid; crystal violet – antiseptic; quinine – antimalarial.
33-028.t: Analgesic relieves pain; anaesthetic causes loss of sensation.

33-029.r: Sedative → potassium bromide (KBr), used as anticonvulsant and sedative in the late 19th and early 20th centuries; now an antiepileptic for dogs.

33-030.r: Carbon monoxide (CO) → forms a stable, irreversible complex with haemoglobin, carboxyhaemoglobin (COHb); colourless, odourless gas from incomplete burning of fuels.

33-031.r: Homogenized milk → fat broken into microscopic particles so it no longer separates; a purely physical process, nothing is added.

33-032.r: Active component of clove oil → eugenol, a colourless to light yellow aromatic oily liquid with a spicy clove smell.

33-033.r: Fruit best for jelly making → guava, because of its high pectin (and acid) content.

33-034.r: Organic food → grown without artificial fertilizers and most conventional pesticides; no sewage sludge, bioengineering or ionizing radiation.

34-001.r: Soap → vegetable oil (or animal fat) + caustic soda; olive, palm kernel and coconut oils are used.

34-002.r: Soap removes grease by emulsification: its long hydrocarbon chain dissolves in grease, the polar COO–Na+ end dissolves in water.

34-003.r: Detergent → book's answer: refining agent; a surfactant (or mix of surfactants) with cleaning and refining properties, different from soap.

34-004.r: Laundry detergents → alkylbenzene sulfonates; like soap but more soluble in hard water.

34-005.r: A true: detergent removes oil and dirt easily. R false: detergent REDUCES, not increases, the surface tension of water.

34-006.r: Synthetic detergents lather in hard water because they form soluble calcium and magnesium salts (no insoluble precipitate) → A and R true, R explains A.

34-007.r: In washing powder → sodium sulphate maintains basicity; sodium silicate makes the powder crystalline so it stays dry → both statements correct.

35-001.r: One metric ton of organic manure gives only about 1.5 to 3 kg phosphorus → chemical fertilizers needed for phosphorus. A and R true, R explains A.

35-002.r: Wheat cultivation → nitrogen fertilizer most important for growth; nitrogen deficiency is the most common plant nutrient problem.

35-003.r: Not supplied by fertilizers → hydrogen; carbon, hydrogen, oxygen come from CO2 and water. Of at least 16 essential elements, N, P, K, chlorine etc. come from soil.

35-004.r: The book gives no single answer (*): all pairs are correct: nitrogen → growth; phosphorus → root development; potassium → stomatal opening/closing; boron → disease resistance.

35-005.r: Fertilizer leaving most soil acidity → ammonium sulphate (most acidifying nitrogen fertilizer; not advised on acidic soils). Acidic soil has pH below 7.

35-006.r: Urea → nitrogen-containing organic compound, CO(NH2)2, also called carbamide; about 46% nitrogen in amide form.
35-006.t: Urea is an organic compound, not an inorganic one or a plant hormone.

35-007.r: Nitrogen in urea (carbamide, CO(NH2)2) → about 46%, option 47%; elements C, H, N, O; nitrogen in amide (NH2) form.

35-010.r: Most water-soluble fertilizer at 20°C (of options) → urea; name from Greek 'oura' = urine.

35-011.r: Urea for 1 kg nitrogen → 100/46 × 1000 g ≈ 2174 g ≈ 2.2 kg (urea has about 46% N).

35-012.r: True: ammonia (urea input) is made from natural gas; sulfur for phosphoric acid fertilizer is a refinery by-product. False: urea's MRP is fixed by Government → 2, 3.

35-013.r: Excess nitrogenous fertilizer → soil acidity and nitrate leaching to groundwater (also eutrophication); it does not multiply nitrogen-fixing microbes → 2 and 3.

35-014.r: Urea manufacture → synthetic ammonia + carbon dioxide; CO2 is consumed.

35-015.r: Neem-coated urea → neem oil slows urea's dissolution and nitrification (nitrification inhibitor), so nitrogen releases gradually and less escapes; higher yields.

35-016.r: DAP (diammonium phosphate) → 18% nitrogen and 46% P2O5; solution pH about 7.5–8.

35-017.r: Mixed (complex) fertilizer → NPK, with nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium in different ratios; urea, CAN, ammonium sulphate are not mixed.

35-018.r: Not a chemical fertilizer → sodium sulphate (Na2SO4, sodium salt of sulfuric acid); urea, super phosphate, potassium nitrate are fertilizers.

35-019.r: Most popular fertilizer for foliar application (spray on leaves) → urea: highly soluble and absorbed quickly by leaves.

35-020.r: Humus → organic colloid: dark organic material formed in topsoil when plant and animal matter decays.

35-021.r: Best green manure crop → sunhemp; green manure crops (sunhemp, dhaincha, sesbania) are mostly legumes ploughed into the soil.

36-001.r: Chemistry Nobel 2021 → Benjamin List & David MacMillan (asymmetric organocatalysis). 2023 → quantum dots; 2024 → David Baker, Hassabis, Jumper (proteins); 2025 → metal-organic frameworks.

36-002.r: Chemistry Nobel 2019 → lithium-ion batteries (Goodenough, Whittingham, Yoshino); 2020 → Charpentier & Doudna, CRISPR/Cas9 genome editing.

36-003.r: UV-cutting glass → Crookes glass (mainly cerium oxide + silica), used in sunglasses. Pyrex → low-expansion borosilicate; Jena → shock- and heat-resistant.

36-004.r: Hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs) → used in aerosols, foam agents and fire retardants (fire protection), but not to make lubricants → only three.

36-005.r: Ozone layer destroyer → chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs); one chlorine atom can destroy over 100,000 ozone molecules in the stratosphere.

36-006.r: Ozone (O3) kills microorganisms in water as a powerful oxidizing agent; it is not radioactive, but that is not the reason → A and R true, R not explanation.

36-007.r: Fire alarm → photocell, using the photoelectric effect; its resistance changes with the light falling on it.

36-008.r: Gas in fire extinguishers → carbon dioxide (CO2), for controlling small fires.

36-009.r: Ordinary (soda-acid) extinguisher → CO2 from sodium bicarbonate + dilute sulfuric acid: 2NaHCO3 + H2SO4 → Na2SO4 + 2H2O + 2CO2.

36-010.r: Soda-acid fire extinguisher → sodium bicarbonate solution (the 'soda') + dilute sulfuric acid (the 'acid'); the CO2 formed cuts off oxygen.

36-012.r: Active chemical against mosquitoes → allethrin, a synthetic pyrethroid insecticide.

36-013.r: Prallethrin → pyrethroid mosquito repellent; 1.6% w/w liquid vaporizers (e.g. Good Knight, All Out).

36-014.r: Mosquito repellent → pyrethrum, a natural botanical insecticide that acts on the insects' nervous system.

36-015.r: Pyrethrin in mosquito coils → from a seed plant, Chrysanthemum cinerariifolium.

36-016.r: Natural mosquito repellent → lemongrass (citronella or fever grass), source of citronella oil used in repellents, sprays and candles.

36-017.r: Rat poison (rodenticide) → potassium cyanide (KCN) and zinc phosphide, both highly toxic.

36-020.r: The book gives no single answer (*): aluminium phosphide, a cheap pesticide releasing toxic phosphine gas, is used as fumigant for stored cereals and as rodenticide.

36-021.r: Herbicide (weedkiller) → sodium chlorate (NaClO3), an oxidizing agent.

36-022.r: Carbofuran, methyl parathion, phorate, triazophos → farm pesticides; Pesticides (Prohibition) Order, 2018 (Anupam Verma Committee) banned 18 pesticides, including the last three.

36-023.r: Weedicide for paddy → 2,4-D (2,4-dichlorophenoxyacetic acid), a selective translocated herbicide for broadleaf weeds.

36-024.r: 2,4-D → herbicide (systemic, for broadleaf weeds); it is a synthetic auxin (plant hormone), also used in plant cell culture media.
